Itch
ICH
n. (an irritating skin sensation causing a desire to scratch; a covenant curse named among the diseases of Deuteronomy)
Saxon giccan, to itch. The Authorized Version's one literal use names an actual skin affliction; its one figurative use, centuries later in English translation, borrows the same sensation for an appetite that cannot leave sound doctrine alone.

Biblical Definition

Deuteronomy's covenant curses, spoken before Israel ever crossed the Jordan, include the itch among a short list of afflictions attached to covenant unfaithfulness: The LORD will smite thee with the botch of Egypt, and with the emerods, and with the scab, and with the itch, whereof thou canst not be healed. The itch here is named alongside diseases Israel had already seen firsthand in Egypt, redirected now as a possible covenant consequence rather than a plague inflicted on an enemy — the same LORD who once smote Egypt for Israel's sake could smite Israel herself if the covenant were broken, and this particular affliction is marked as one whereof thou canst not be healed, incurable by any human remedy.

Second Timothy borrows the same sensation for an entirely different but structurally similar condition: a time will come when men after their own lusts shall heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears, unable to endure sound doctrine and instead accumulating teachers who will scratch the specific itch their own lusts demand. The physical itch of Deuteronomy and the itching ears of Timothy share exactly the trait that makes the figure work: an itch does not resolve itself by being scratched, it only demands to be scratched again, and a congregation gathering teachers to match its own cravings is describing a condition, not a cure.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): an uneasy sensation in the skin, exciting a desire to scratch; a cutaneous disease attended by such sensation.

expand to see more

ITCH, n. A cutaneous disease, marked by a troublesome sensation and eruption; also, an uneasy desire or craving.

BOTCH, n. A large ulcerous swelling; a boil; a plague sore.

SCAB, n. A crust formed over a healing sore; also, a disease of animals affecting the skin.

HEAL, v.t. To cure of a disease or wound; to restore to soundness.

SOUND, a. Free from defect, error or disease; whole; healthy; here, of doctrine, free from corruption or falsehood.

Key Scripture

Deu 28:15 — "But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee:"

Deu 28:27 — "The LORD will smite thee with the botch of Egypt, and with the emerods, and with the scab, and with the itch, whereof thou canst not be healed."

2Ti 4:3 — "For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;"

2Ti 4:4 — "And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables."

Modern Corruption

Itching ears are treated as simple curiosity or a taste for variety, when Paul names it a symptom of a specific inability to endure sound doctrine, matched by teachers gathered deliberately to feed the craving rather than to cure it.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the physical word, but the figurative use in 2 Timothy names a temptation that has only grown more efficient with time: the deliberate cultivation of teachers who will say exactly what a listener's own lusts already wanted to hear, so that no doctrine ever has to be endured, only agreed with in advance.

Deuteronomy's itch is instructive precisely because it is named as incurable by human means — whereof thou canst not be healed — and the figurative itch of 2 Timothy carries the same structure. A congregation that heaps up teachers to match its cravings is not thereby satisfied; it has simply institutionalized the itch, guaranteeing a fresh supply of scratching and no possibility of the only real cure, sound doctrine received rather than curated.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew garab (H1618), an itch, a scab; one item in the covenant curse list of Deuteronomy 28:27; Greek knetho (G2833), to itch, to tickle, behind Paul's figure in 2 Timothy 4:3.

expand to see more

Hebrew garab (H1618) — the itch, a scab or eruption; the noun of Deuteronomy 28:27, listed among covenant-curse diseases.

Hebrew shechiyn (H7822) — a boil, a botch; the disease named first in the same verse, elsewhere the affliction of Job.

Greek knetho (G2833) — to itch, to tickle, to scratch; the participle behind “itching” in 2 Timothy 4:3, used only here in the New Testament.

Greek episoreuo (G2002) — to heap up, to accumulate; the verb behind “heap to themselves teachers.”

Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, healthy, whole; the standing New Testament word for sound doctrine, the very thing itching ears cannot endure.

Usage

"“the LORD will smite thee... with the itch, whereof thou canst not be healed” — the covenant curse of Deuteronomy."

"“having itching ears” — Paul's figure for a craving no true doctrine can satisfy."

"“heap to themselves teachers... after their own lusts” — the deliberate feeding of that craving."
